**The Weight of a Name**

The first time I saw the name *Elias Voss* carved into the oak door of the old library, I knew it wasn’t just a name. It was a promise—or a warning. The wood had been polished to a deep, almost black sheen, the letters sharp enough to cut. I traced the curve of the *S* with my fingertip, feeling the grain resist me, as if the name itself was alive.

I was twelve when my mother died. Not from illness, not from accident—from something worse. A name. Or rather, the absence of one. She had been *Lena* before she married my father, but after he died, she became *Mrs. Elias Voss* by default. The name stuck to her like a second skin, even when she stopped answering to it. The last time I saw her, she was standing in the kitchen, staring at the stove as if it might burn her alive. She said, *"They’ll take it from you one day, you know. The name. The house. Everything."* Then she turned off the gas and walked out.

I didn’t understand then what she meant. Now, standing in this library, I do.

The door creaked open before I could push it. The air inside was thick with the scent of old paper and something sharper—ozone, maybe, or the faint metallic tang of fear. The shelves were floor-to-ceiling, their spines lined up like soldiers. Most of the books were in German, their titles in elegant script that made my stomach twist. But one shelf, near the back, held English volumes. *The Art of Forgetting. How to Lose a Name. The Silent Ledger.*

I pulled out the last one. The cover was cracked, the pages yellowed at the edges. Inside, the first entry read:

*"Elias Voss was not his real name. He was born *Elias Roth*, but the name was taken from him when he was twelve. The man who did it was a collector. He didn’t just want Elias’s name—he wanted his *story*. His father had been a thief, his mother a liar. Elias was the only one left who could tell the truth. But truth, as Elias learned, is a currency. And collectors always pay in blood."*

I flipped to the next page. A sketch of a man with hollow cheeks and eyes like flint. The caption read: *"The Collector. He never signed his name. He only left his mark."*

My hands were shaking. I should have put the book back. I should have walked away. But the library had a way of holding you, of making you forget the world outside its walls.

The door slammed shut behind me.

I spun around. No one was there.

Then I heard it—the whisper of turning pages. Not from the book in my hands. From the shelves.

I ran.

The exit was a narrow alley, the kind that smelled of damp stone and something older, something *wrong*. At the end of it stood a black car, its windows tinted so dark I couldn’t see inside. The engine was running.

A voice, smooth as oil, cut through the night. *"You shouldn’t have come back."*

I turned. A man stood in the doorway of the library, his face half-hidden in shadow. He was tall, his suit immaculate, his hands folded in front of him like a man who had nothing to fear. But his eyes—oh, his eyes were *hungry*.

*"You’re Elias Voss,"* he said. *"Or at least, you were."*

I backed up. *"Who are you?"*

He smiled. It wasn’t a friendly smile. It was the smile of a man who had just been handed a debt. *"The Collector’s son."*

The car’s headlights flared to life. The engine revved.

I ran.

---

**The Library of Lost Names**

They say the first library was built not to store knowledge, but to *preserve* it. To keep the names of the dead from being erased. But some names refuse to stay buried.

I found out the hard way.

It started with the books. Not the ones on the shelves, but the ones *between* them—the gaps where titles had been torn out, pages missing, as if someone had taken them by force. The librarian, an old woman with silver hair and a face like carved stone, just shrugged when I asked about them. *"Some things,"* she said, *"are better left unread."*

Then came the dreams.

In them, I was always twelve again. Running through corridors lined with books, my mother’s voice echoing behind me: *"They’ll take it from you."* The doors would slam shut, the shelves would shift, and I’d wake up gasping, my sheets damp with sweat, my name written in something darker than ink on my wrist.

The third night, I dreamed of Elias Voss.

He wasn’t a boy in the dream. He was a man, standing in a room filled with ledgers. Each one was a name, a life, a story. And the Collector was there, his hand outstretched, his voice a velvet promise: *"You can have it back. All of it."*

Elias laughed. It was a bitter sound. *"Names aren’t things you can just take back. They’re what’s left when everything else is gone."*

I woke up screaming.

---

**The Ledger**

I found it tucked inside the last book I stole from the library. A small, leather-bound journal, its cover worn smooth by time. The first entry was dated 1893.

*"Today, Elias Roth was born. His father was a thief, his mother a liar. His name was a lie before he even knew what a name was. But names matter. They are the first thing they take. The last thing they leave."*

I turned the page.

*"The Collector came at midnight. He didn’t ask. He just took. Elias’s father tried to fight. The Collector laughed. ‘Names are easier than blood,’ he said. Elias watched as his father’s hands turned black, as his mouth stretched too wide, as his name—*Jacob Roth*—slipped from his lips like smoke. Elias screamed. The Collector smiled. ‘Now you’re just Elias,’ he said. ‘And Elias is mine.’"*

I closed the book. My hands were trembling.

The librarian found me the next morning, sitting in the reading room, the journal clutched to my chest. She didn’t ask how I got it. She just handed me a slip of paper.

*"The exit is always where you least expect it,"* she said. *"But remember—names are not just words. They are the only thing that makes you *you*."*

I looked at the paper. It was a map. To the library’s basement.

I didn’t go.

---

**The Truth About Names**

Names are not just labels. They are contracts. Promises. Curses.

My mother was right. They *will* take it from you.

But here’s the secret no one tells you: you can take it back.

It’s not easy. It’s not clean. It’s messy, like tearing off a bandage too fast. But it’s yours.

I spent the next week in the library, poring over ledgers, memorizing names, tracing the threads of lies that bound them. I learned that Elias Voss wasn’t just a name—he was a *chain*. And the Collector had been collecting them for generations.

On the seventh night, I stood in the basement, the air thick with dust and something older, something *hungry*. The walls were lined with shelves, but these shelves held no books. They held *things*—small, blackened objects, each one a name, a life, a story stolen.

And at the center of it all was the Collector’s throne.

A man sat there, his back to me. He was old now, his skin like parchment, his eyes hollow. But his voice was still smooth, still dangerous.

*"You’ve been a very good little thief,"* he said. *"But names are not toys. They are *power*."*

I stepped forward. *"I don’t want power. I want my mother’s name back."*

He turned. His face was a mask of disappointment. *"Oh, child. You don’t understand. Names are not given. They are *taken*. And once they are taken, they are *mine*."*

I reached into my pocket. My fingers closed around the journal—the one with Elias’s story. I held it up.

*"Then I’ll take it back."*

The Collector laughed. It was the sound of a man who had just been handed a chess piece he didn’t want. *"You can’t. Not without blood."*

I opened the journal to the last page. It was blank.

I wrote my name in it.

Then I tore it out.

The Collector’s eyes widened. *"No—"*

I hurled the paper at him.

It hit him square in the chest. For a moment, nothing happened. Then his skin *ripped*, like wet paper. His mouth stretched too wide, his teeth blackening, his voice twisting into something not quite human.

*"You fool,"* he hissed. *"Names are not just words. They are *identity*. And identity is *mine*."*

I ran.

The basement doors slammed shut behind me. I could hear him—laughing, screaming, *feeding*—as I stumbled up the stairs, my lungs burning, my heart pounding.

I burst into the library, gasping. The shelves were empty. The books were gone. The librarian was gone.

Only the door remained.

And on it, in fresh, bleeding letters, was a new name:

**ELIAS VOSS**

I touched it. The wood was warm.

I smiled.

Because names are not just words.

They are the only thing that makes you *you*.

And I was taking mine back.

---

**Epilogue: The Collector’s Ledger**

*(Found in the ruins of the library, years later. The ink is fresh, the handwriting frantic.)*

*"They always think they can take it back. The name. The life. The *them*. But names are not just words. They are *power*. And power is not given. It is *taken*.

*Elias Voss was mine. He took it back. But names are not just names. They are *contracts*. And contracts must be paid in full.

*I will find him. And when I do, I will remind him of the truth: names are not just words. They are the only thing that makes you *you*.

*And I will take it all back."*

*(The last entry is smudged, as if written in haste.)*

*"He’s coming."*

*(The page is torn from the ledger.)*
